title: Check yourself: The identifier boundary, the audit log and the practice

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Scenario: Fennel Health's drafting assistant receives claim notes with patient names, contact details and policy numbers. Which design best keeps these away from the model provider?

options.text: A system prompt that instructs the model to ignore any personal details it comes across
options.says: Ruled out because "the data has already crossed the boundary".

options.text: A review step that checks the model's reply for personal details after it has been returned
options.says: Ruled out because a check on the reply, like an instruction, "acts after the data has already crossed the boundary".

options.text: A larger model that is better at noticing which parts of a note are sensitive ones
options.says: Ruled out because the model would still receive the data, and the point is to keep the identifier out of the request: "It cannot leak what it never had".

options.text: A layer that tokenises identifiers before the call and restores them afterwards
options.says: A layer before the call means the provider sees tokens and never the values, and the layer can be tested.

origin.section: The identifier boundary, the audit log and the practice

questions.stem: Scenario: Rook Mutual's auditors ask for proof of each model call. The team proposes logging every full prompt and reply for ten years. What should the architect say?

options.text: Log request identifiers, sizes and outcomes, and keep content in the system of record
options.says: The log proves what happened without becoming a second copy of the data.

options.text: Accept the proposal, since a complete record is the strongest evidence that a regulator can ask to see
options.says: Ruled out because "the log becomes a second store of sensitive data with its own obligations".

options.text: Log full content, but encrypt the log, which removes the obligations that a data store has
options.says: Ruled out because encryption protects a store and does not remove it: the log would still be "a store of health or personal data, with all the obligations of one".

options.text: Log nothing from the calls, since any stored record of a call becomes a risk in itself
options.says: Ruled out because an audit log must record "who, when, which request and what size".
